title: Typed Arrays and Binary Data
description: Model binary memory with ArrayBuffer views, parse byte layouts with DataView, and transfer ownership safely.
learningOutcomes: Distinguish raw ArrayBuffer storage from typed-array views over shared bytes.
Choose integer, floating-point, clamped, or DataView access based on the format contract.
Explain byte offsets, element indexes, overflow/conversion, and endianness.
Transfer a buffer to a worker and recognize that the sender's buffer is detached.

blocks.text: Binary data is bytes plus an interpretation

An ArrayBuffer is a fixed-length region of raw bytes. It does not say whether those bytes represent pixels, audio samples, an integer, or text. A typed array creates a view that interprets aligned groups of bytes as numeric elements; a DataView reads and writes fields at explicit byte offsets. This separation matters whenever you decode files, protocols, media, or worker messages: the format contract—not the JavaScript variable name—defines what each byte means.

items: ArrayBuffer owns the bytes; byteLength measures storage capacity, not the number of values.
TypedArray views share a buffer and provide indexed numeric access; view.byteOffset and view.length describe the view, while view.byteLength describes its span.
DataView is useful for mixed field widths and explicit endianness; typed-array multi-byte byte order follows the platform.
Multiple views can read or mutate the same bytes, so aliasing and offsets are part of correctness.

steps.title: Allocate bytes, not values
steps.explanation: The buffer reserves eight bytes. It has no built-in type or element count.

steps.title: Create two views over the same storage
steps.explanation: Uint8Array sees each byte. Uint16Array starts at byte offset 2 and reads two 16-bit elements; its offset must satisfy alignment.

steps.title: Observe aliasing and byte order
steps.explanation: Writing bytes 2 and 3 changes the first word view. Its numeric value depends on host byte order, so do not use typed arrays alone to define a portable file or network format.

steps.title: Keep units explicit
steps.explanation: byteLength counts bytes; length counts elements; byteOffset is measured in bytes. Mixing these units is a common source of off-by-two bugs.

blocks.text: Typed arrays convert assigned values to their element representation. Integer arrays truncate fractional parts and wrap values to the representable range; Uint8ClampedArray instead clamps and rounds into 0–255. Float32Array can round values to a lower-precision representation. If input is untrusted or must be rejected when out of range, validate it before assigning—typed-array conversion silently changes it.

blocks.prompt: What does assigning 258 to a Uint8Array element do?

options.text: It throws RangeError because the value exceeds 255.
options.feedback: Typed-array element assignment converts the value rather than validating the domain.

options.text: It stores 258 exactly using extra bytes.
options.feedback: A Uint8Array element is one byte and cannot represent 258 as an unsigned 8-bit value.

options.text: It wraps into the 8-bit range, producing 2.
options.feedback: Correct. Uint8 conversion keeps the low eight bits; use explicit validation if overflow should be rejected.
Clamping is the behavior of Uint8ClampedArray, not Uint8Array.

blocks.explanation: Typed-array assignment applies numeric conversion rules; it is not a range check. Choose clamping or explicit validation according to the data contract.

blocks.text: Use DataView for portable mixed-field layouts

blocks.code:
const buffer = new ArrayBuffer(5);
const view = new DataView(buffer);

view.setUint16(0, 0x1234);       // big-endian by default
view.setUint8(2, 3);             // version byte
view.setUint16(3, 0x1234, true); // little-endian explicitly

console.log(view.getUint16(0));       // 0x1234
console.log(view.getUint8(2));        // 3
console.log(view.getUint16(3, true)); // 0x1234

steps.title: Treat offsets as byte positions
steps.explanation: DataView can read mixed-width values from one buffer. Its offsets always count bytes.

steps.title: Declare byte order for the format
steps.explanation: DataView multi-byte methods default to big-endian; pass true for little-endian. Specify the format explicitly instead of relying on a machine's native order.

steps.title: Read with the same layout contract
steps.explanation: A field must be decoded with the same width, offset, signedness, and endianness used by the producer. Invalid offsets can throw RangeError.

blocks.title: Protocol layout is a contract
blocks.text: Before parsing bytes, check the input is long enough for every field and reject unknown versions or impossible lengths. DataView accessors do not validate the meaning of values, and a valid numeric read does not make an untrusted file safe.

blocks.prompt: A file format specifies a 16-bit little-endian length at byte offset 4. Which read matches that contract?

options.feedback: Without the second argument DataView uses big-endian for this accessor.
Correct. Offsets count bytes, and true requests little-endian interpretation.
8 would be a different byte offset; a 16-bit field does not make you multiply the offset by two.
The index counts 16-bit elements, not bytes, and the view's byte order is platform-dependent.

blocks.explanation: Match the external layout exactly: byte offset 4, unsigned 16-bit width, little-endian order.

blocks.text: Transfer buffers when moving large payloads

steps.title: Create a large byte payload
steps.explanation: A typed view is a convenient way to edit the buffer, but the view and the buffer are distinct objects.

steps.title: Transfer ownership explicitly
steps.explanation: The transfer list moves the ArrayBuffer instead of cloning its bytes. The sender's buffer is detached and cannot be reused; plan ownership before sending.

steps.title: Recreate a view in the receiver
steps.explanation: The worker gets the transferred buffer and constructs a new view. Do not keep using the sender's old view after transfer.

blocks.title: SharedArrayBuffer is a different concurrency model
blocks.text: A SharedArrayBuffer is visible to multiple agents rather than transferred. Shared writes can race; synchronization with Atomics and cross-origin isolation requirements are involved. Prefer ordinary transferable ArrayBuffers unless shared concurrent access is a measured requirement.

blocks.title: Decode a compact packet header
blocks.context: A telemetry packet starts with the magic value 0xCAFE as 16-bit big-endian, a one-byte version, a one-byte flags field, and a 16-bit little-endian payload length. Decode it defensively before reading the payload.
instructions: Implement `decodeHeader(buffer)` using DataView and byte offsets.
Reject a buffer shorter than six bytes, an magic value other than 0xCAFE, an version other than 1, and a declared payload length larger than the bytes remaining.
Return named fields without copying the payload unnecessarily; use a Uint8Array view with the correct byteOffset and length.
Add tests for valid input, truncated header, wrong magic, version other than 1, and oversized length.
Explain why DataView is used for the header and why the payload can remain a byte view.
requirements: Use `DataView(buffer, byteOffset, byteLength)` or an equivalent bounded view.
Specify endianness explicitly for both multi-byte fields.
Check bounds before reading and before constructing the payload view.
Do not assume typed-array element index equals byte offset.
Never silently clamp or wrap invalid header values.
hints: DataView offsets are bytes; the first 16-bit field occupies offsets 0–1.
The payload starts at byte 6; compare its declared length to buffer.byteLength - 6.
A little-endian length uses the optional second argument true.
Construct Uint8Array(buffer, 6, payloadLength) only after validating the range.
successCriteria: Valid packet fields match the 0xCAFE magic and version 1/flags/length.
Every multi-byte read uses the defined byte order explicitly.
Truncated and unsupported input is rejected with a useful error.
Oversized declared length is rejected before constructing a view.
Payload view points to the original buffer without an unnecessary copy.
Tests cover each invalid condition and explain byte-offset units.
